passages.title: The Bakery That Went Online
paragraphs: For twenty years, Rosa's Bakery sold bread the same way: customers walked in, pointed at a loaf, and paid at the counter. Then the road outside the shop closed for repairs, and for six months almost no one could reach it.
Rosa's daughter, Lina, had an idea. She built a simple website where people could order bread the night before, and each morning she delivered the orders to customers' homes in the family van.

At first, only a few people used it, and Rosa worried that the plan would fail. But Lina posted photos of fresh bread on the bakery's page every day, and slowly the orders grew. Some customers liked knowing their bread was saved for them, while others liked not having to wait in line.

Something else changed, too. Because people ordered ahead, Rosa knew exactly how many loaves to bake. Before, she often threw away a third of her bread at the end of the day; now she threw away almost none.

When the road finally reopened, Rosa expected everything to go back to normal, but it didn't. Half of her customers kept ordering online. Rosa still loves chatting with people at the counter, but she admits the website taught her something important. Sometimes a problem pushes you to discover a better way.

questions.stem: Before the website, about how much bread did Rosa throw away at the end of the day?
questions.why: Paragraph 4: she often threw away a third of her bread.

questions.stem: In the last paragraph, what does admits mean?
questions.why: Rosa agrees, maybe a little reluctantly, that the website taught her something.

questions.stem: Why did half of the customers keep ordering online after the road opened?
options: They found it easier than coming in
The counter was often closed early
The bread online cost less money
Lina gave them free delivery coupons
questions.why: Paragraph 3 gives the reasons: bread saved for them and no line. Nothing says the price was lower.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: A problem led the bakery to a better way of selling.
Road repairs can ruin a small business for good.
Selling bread online costs more than selling in a shop.
Lina wanted to take over her mother's bakery soon.
questions.why: The closed road pushed the bakery online, and the new way worked better.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention the photos Lina posted?
options: To show how the orders slowly grew
To explain why the road was closed
To show that Rosa took the photos
To prove it was the best bread in town
questions.why: The photos come right before "slowly the orders grew."

passages.title: Hiding in Plain Sight
paragraphs: An octopus has no shell and no sharp teeth to protect it, and its soft body makes an easy meal for many hungry animals. So how does it survive? It hides in plain sight.

An octopus can change the color of its skin in less than a second. Its skin contains thousands of tiny sacs filled with color, and muscles surrounding each sac can stretch it open to display the color or squeeze it shut to hide it. By opening some sacs and closing others, an octopus can create spots, stripes, or a plain dark brown.

Color is only part of the trick, because an octopus can also raise small bumps on its skin. When it settles on a rock, the bumps make its skin look rough, exactly like the rock itself, so a fish swimming past may notice nothing but stone.

One question still puzzles scientists. Most octopuses seem to see the world without much color, yet they match their surroundings remarkably well. Some researchers think their skin may sense light directly, while others believe octopuses match patterns and brightness rather than exact colors. No one knows for sure yet.

questions.stem: What makes an octopus's skin look rough like a rock?
options: Bumps it raises on its skin
Sand that sticks to its body
Dark spots that cover its arms
Tiny sacs that fill with color
questions.why: Paragraph 3: it raises small bumps that make its skin look rough.

questions.stem: In paragraph 1, what does survive mean?
questions.why: The question is how a soft animal with no shell stays alive.

questions.stem: Why might a fish swim right past an octopus?
options: It can't tell it apart from the rock
It is afraid of the octopus's teeth
It only ever hunts for food at night
The octopus is much too large to eat
questions.why: The octopus looks like stone. The passage says it has no sharp teeth.

questions.stem: What is the passage mostly about?
options: How an octopus hides by changing its skin
Why octopuses see the world without color
Which animals hunt octopuses in the sea
How scientists study animals in the ocean
questions.why: Every paragraph is about how the octopus hides. Color vision is one puzzle at the end.

questions.stem: Why does the author end with what scientists don't know?
options: To show a mystery is still unsolved
To prove that octopuses can see color
To argue that scientists made a mistake
To explain how the color sacs work
questions.why: The last paragraph presents an open question: no one knows for sure yet.

passages.title: Four Days a Week
paragraphs: When Harbor Tools announced that it would experiment with a four-day workweek, many employees assumed there was a catch. Would they have to work ten-hour days? Would their pay be reduced? The answer to both questions was no: for six months, the company's 140 workers would work four eight-hour days and keep their full salaries.

The company's leaders had a practical reason for the experiment. Hiring had become increasingly difficult, and experienced workers kept leaving for competitors. A shorter week, they hoped, would make Harbor Tools a place where people wanted to stay.

To make the plan work, every team had to identify wasted time. Meetings were shortened from an hour to thirty minutes, and workers stopped copying the entire office on routine emails. One team discovered that it spent most of every Monday morning fixing problems that a simple checklist could prevent.
The results surprised even the skeptics. Output remained about the same, fewer people quit, and sick days dropped by nearly a third.

Not everyone was satisfied, however. The customer service team struggled, because customers still expected help five days a week. The company eventually divided that team into two groups with different days off, so the phones were always covered. The managers acknowledged that the schedule worked better for some jobs than for others.

At the end of the trial, Harbor Tools voted to keep the four-day week. It also kept the checklist, the shorter meetings, and the smaller email lists, changes that some employees say mattered almost as much as the extra day off.

questions.stem: How did the company keep the phones covered?
options: It split the team into two groups
It hired workers just for Fridays
It sent calls to another company
It let some calls go to voicemail
questions.why: Paragraph 5: it split the customer service team into two groups.

questions.stem: In paragraph 4, what does skeptics mean?
questions.why: Paragraph 1 describes workers who assumed there was a catch. The results surprised the doubters.

questions.stem: Why did the managers likely care that fewer people quit?
options: Keeping workers was the trial's goal
They planned to cut every worker's pay
Workers who quit had taken company tools
Fewer workers meant fewer long meetings
questions.why: Paragraph 2: good workers kept leaving, and the shorter week was meant to make them stay.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the main idea?
options: A four-day week worked, partly because it made teams cut wasted time.
A four-day week failed because customers still called five days a week.
Harbor Tools cut its workers' hours and their pay for six months.
Most workers prefer ten-hour days to a standard five-day week.
questions.why: The trial succeeded, and the last paragraph credits the time-saving changes too.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the paragraph about customer service?
options: To show that the plan also had downsides
To explain why the trial was ended early
To prove that customers disliked the change
To describe how the trial was first planned
questions.why: It starts "Not everyone was happy" and shows a problem the company had to solve.

passages.title: Clinton's Ditch
paragraphs: In 1817, New York began digging a canal across the entire state, from the Hudson River at Albany to Lake Erie at Buffalo. Many people considered the idea foolish. The canal would stretch 363 miles through forests and swamps, and it would have to climb hills that boats could not float up on their own. Critics mockingly called it "Clinton's Ditch," after the governor who championed it.

Workers dug most of the canal by hand, using shovels, horses, and simple machines designed for pulling up tree stumps. To carry boats over the hills, engineers built locks, which are chambers that fill with water to raise a boat or drain to lower it.

When the canal opened in 1825, it transformed the country's economy almost overnight. Before, moving a ton of goods from Buffalo to New York City by wagon cost about $100 and took weeks; by canal, it cost about $10 and took days. Farmers in the Midwest could now sell their grain in eastern cities, and factories in the East could ship tools and cloth to the growing West.

New York City benefited most of all. Goods from the entire Great Lakes region now flowed through its harbor, and it soon became the busiest port in the nation. Towns along the canal, such as Rochester and Syracuse, also grew rapidly.
The "ditch" that critics had ridiculed turned out to be one of the most successful public projects of its era.

questions.stem: What did the locks do?
options: Raised and lowered boats over hills
Kept water from leaking into swamps
Stopped boats from passing at night
Pulled tree stumps out of the ground
questions.why: Paragraph 2: locks fill or drain to raise or lower a boat.

questions.stem: In paragraph 1, what does critics mean?
options: people who found fault with it
people who paid to build it
people who worked on the canal
people who lived near the route
questions.why: They called the plan foolish and mocked it as a ditch.

questions.stem: Why did the canal help farmers in the Midwest?
options: Shipping grain east got far cheaper
The canal watered their dry fields
Eastern cities paid them to move east
The canal let them stop growing grain
questions.why: Moving a ton of goods dropped from about $100 to about $10.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: A canal many doubted changed trade in America.
Building canals by hand was dangerous and slow work.
Governor Clinton was disliked by most New Yorkers.
Rochester and Syracuse were founded as canal towns.
questions.why: It goes from doubts, to building, to a big change in trade.

questions.stem: Why does the author compare the cost of shipping by wagon and by canal?
options: To show how much the canal lowered costs
To explain why the canal took years to build
To show that wagons were faster than boats
To argue that the canal cost too much
questions.why: The numbers show the cost falling to a tenth.

passages.title: The Empty Seat Problem
paragraphs: Airlines routinely sell more tickets than there are seats on a plane. To many travelers, this practice seems unfair, even dishonest. Yet from the airline's point of view, overbooking is a calculated response to a predictable problem: on almost every flight, some passengers who bought tickets never show up.

An empty seat on a departing plane is lost revenue that can never be recovered. Unlike a sweater in a store, a seat cannot be sold tomorrow. If an airline knows from years of data that roughly one in twenty passengers on a certain route misses the flight, it can sell a few extra tickets and expect the plane to leave full.

The strategy depends on accurate forecasts. Business travelers on Monday morning flights rarely miss them, while travelers on holiday routes may change plans more often. Airlines therefore adjust how many extra seats they sell for each route, day, and season.

When the forecast is wrong and too many passengers arrive, the airline must find volunteers to give up their seats, usually by offering travel vouchers or cash. If no one volunteers, some passengers can be bumped against their will, and regulations require the airline to compensate them.
For the airline, these payments are a cost of doing business, one that is usually smaller than the revenue lost by flying with empty seats. For the stranded traveler, the math offers little comfort.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why do airlines change how many extra tickets they sell?
options: No-show rates differ by route and season
Regulations limit sales on some routes
Holiday flights tend to use larger planes
questions.why: Paragraph 3: they adjust by route, day and season because no-show rates differ.

questions.stem: In paragraph 2, what does revenue mean?
questions.why: An unsold seat is money the airline never earns.

questions.stem: Which flight would an airline probably overbook the least?
options: A flight during a holiday week
A flight with cheap flexible fares
questions.why: Business travelers on Monday mornings rarely miss flights, so fewer extra tickets are needed.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Overbooking is a planned bet that some passengers won't show.
Airlines overbook because their planes are too small for demand.
Most passengers who are bumped receive no compensation at all.
Business travelers cause most of the problems with overbooking.
questions.why: The passage explains overbooking as a calculated response to predictable no-shows.

questions.stem: Why does the author compare a plane seat to a sweater in a store?
options: To show that an unsold seat's value is lost
To show that seats cost more than clothing
To suggest airlines should lower their fares
To explain how stores also overbook items
questions.why: A sweater can be sold tomorrow; a seat on a flight that has left cannot.

passages.title: Islands of Heat
paragraphs: On a summer evening, a city can be several degrees warmer than the farmland surrounding it. Scientists call this phenomenon an urban heat island, and it is caused largely by the materials and design of cities themselves.

Most urban surfaces are dark and hard. Asphalt streets and tar roofs absorb sunlight throughout the day and store it as heat; after sunset, they gradually release that heat back into the air, which is why the temperature difference between city and countryside is often greatest at night. Concrete and brick behave in a similar way.

Cities also lack something the countryside has in abundance: vegetation. Trees provide shade, and their leaves release water vapor, which cools the surrounding air much as evaporating sweat cools skin. When fields and forests are replaced by parking lots and buildings, both forms of cooling disappear, while cars, factories, and air conditioners contribute additional heat of their own.

The consequences extend well beyond discomfort. Warmer nights make it harder for people to recover from hot days, which is particularly dangerous for older adults and anyone without air conditioning. Higher temperatures also increase electricity consumption, as buildings run their cooling systems longer.

Some cities are responding. They are painting roofs white so that they reflect sunlight instead of absorbing it, planting trees along streets, and covering rooftops with gardens. Each change is modest on its own, but across thousands of buildings, the combined effect can be measurable.

questions.stem: According to the passage, when is the difference between city and countryside often greatest?
questions.why: Paragraph 2: stored heat is released after sunset, so the gap is often greatest at night.

questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does abundance mean?
questions.why: The countryside has plenty of plants; cities lack them.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, a neighborhood that loses most of its trees would probably
options: get more rain than it did before
questions.why: Losing trees removes shade and cooling from leaves, and the passage says heat builds most at night.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Cities run hot because of how they're built, but this can be eased.
Air conditioners are the main reason cities are hotter than farmland.
Rural areas are growing hotter faster than cities in most regions.
White roofs have solved the problem of heat in most large cities.
questions.why: It explains the causes, the harms, and then the fixes.

questions.stem: Why does the author compare leaves to sweat?
options: To explain how plants cool the air
To show that trees need lots of water
To suggest that heat harms people
To describe how plants absorb heat
questions.why: Both release water that cools what's around them.

passages.title: Buying Back the Company
paragraphs: When a company earns more cash than it needs to run its operations, it faces a choice: it can invest in new factories or research, pay its shareholders a dividend, or repurchase some of its own stock. Over the past several decades, buybacks have become an increasingly popular option among large American corporations, and an increasingly controversial one.

The mechanics are straightforward. When a company repurchases its shares, fewer shares remain in the hands of investors. Because the company's profits are now divided among fewer shares, each remaining share represents a larger slice of earnings. Earnings per share, a figure that analysts watch closely, therefore rises, even if total profits have not changed at all.

Supporters argue that buybacks are simply an efficient way to return money to a company's owners. Unlike dividends, which investors come to expect year after year and which companies are therefore reluctant to cut, buybacks can be scaled up or down without alarming the market. A buyback can also signal that executives believe their company's shares are undervalued, since they are willing to spend corporate cash to acquire them.

Critics see a less flattering picture. Cash spent on buybacks is cash not spent on wages, equipment, or research that might strengthen the company over the long term. They also point out that many executives are paid partly in stock, or rewarded for hitting earnings-per-share targets, which gives them a personal incentive to favor buybacks.
Neither side disputes the arithmetic. The disagreement is about priorities: whether a company's spare cash belongs to its current owners or should be invested in its future.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why can buybacks be scaled back more easily than dividends?
options: Investors don't count on them yearly
Buybacks are not reported to analysts
Dividends are set by government rules
questions.why: Paragraph 3: investors come to expect dividends year after year, but not buybacks.

questions.stem: In paragraph 4, what does flattering mean?
questions.why: Critics see a less positive picture than supporters do.

questions.stem: Why might an executive who is rewarded for hitting earnings-per-share targets favor a buyback?
options: It raises that figure even if profits don't
It lowers the amount of tax the company owes
It guarantees that profits will grow next year
It lets the company raise every worker's wages
questions.why: Paragraph 2: fewer shares means higher earnings per share, even with the same profit.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the main idea?
options: Buybacks lift per-share earnings, but whether they're wise is disputed.
Buybacks are banned in most countries because they mislead investors.
Companies should always pay dividends rather than buy back their stock.
Executives mostly use buybacks to raise their own salaries each year.
questions.why: It explains how buybacks work, then lays out both sides without picking one.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the final paragraph?
options: To show the debate is about values, not math
To argue that critics have the stronger case
To explain how buybacks are calculated
To predict that buybacks will soon end
questions.why: "Neither side disputes the arithmetic. The disagreement is about priorities."

passages.title: Bring Back the Walls
paragraphs: For roughly two decades, companies have been tearing down office walls in the name of collaboration. The theory was appealing: place people in one large, open room, and ideas would circulate freely between desks. Executives also noticed a less inspiring advantage, which is that open offices are considerably cheaper, because more employees fit into less space.

That theory deserves reconsideration, because the evidence has not been kind to it. One widely cited study followed employees at two companies as they moved from cubicles into open-plan offices. Rather than talking more, they spoke far less face to face and sent more emails and instant messages instead; surrounded by colleagues, people put on headphones and retreated into their screens.

None of this should surprise anyone who has attempted to write a careful report while a coworker conducts a sales call six feet away. Concentration is fragile, and each interruption carries a cost, measured not only in the minutes lost but in the time required to return to deep focus afterward.

Defenders of the open office are right about one thing: casual encounters matter, and a quick question answered at a neighbor's desk can prevent a day of confusion. But the solution is not to force everyone into permanent proximity. It is to offer people a choice, with quiet rooms for focused work and shared spaces for the conversations that genuinely benefit from them.
Walls, it turns out, were never the obstacle to good teamwork. Constant noise may be.

questions.stem: According to the study, what happened after employees moved into open offices?
options: They talked in person less and messaged more
They talked in person more and messaged less
They asked to move back into cubicles
They finished their projects more quickly
questions.why: Paragraph 2: face-to-face talk fell and emails and messages rose.

questions.stem: In paragraph 4, what does proximity mean?
questions.why: Forcing everyone into permanent closeness, the open room.

questions.stem: What would the author most likely recommend for a team writing a long report?
options: A quiet room away from shared spaces
Desks placed close together for speed
Headphones handed out to every worker
More meetings to share their ideas
questions.why: Paragraph 4: quiet rooms for focused work.

questions.stem: What is the author's main argument?
options: Open offices hurt focus; workers need a choice of spaces.
Open offices are too expensive for most companies to build.
Workers should never talk to each other during the workday.
Cubicles should replace all shared spaces in every office.
questions.why: The author argues against open offices and for a mix of quiet and shared spaces.

questions.stem: Why does the author admit that "casual encounters matter"?
options: To grant a fair point before offering a solution
To show that the study's results were wrong
To argue that open offices should stay as they are
To explain why companies first chose cubicles
questions.why: The author concedes the other side's point, then proposes giving people a choice.

passages.title: The Safety Net Problem
paragraphs: Economists use the term moral hazard to describe a subtle but pervasive problem: when people are protected from the consequences of a risk, they tend to take more of it. The phrase comes from the insurance industry, where underwriters long ago observed that a policyholder whose property was fully insured had less reason to guard it carefully. A homeowner who will be reimbursed for every loss may be less diligent about checking the wiring or locking the doors.

The concept extends well beyond insurance: a bank that expects the government to rescue it in a crisis may make riskier loans, reasoning that it will keep the profits if the gamble succeeds and pass the losses to taxpayers if it fails. Critics of the bailouts that followed the 2008 financial crisis invoked precisely this argument, contending that rescuing large institutions rewarded the very recklessness that had caused the crisis.

Yet moral hazard is easier to identify in theory than to measure in practice. Insured drivers do not, on the whole, appear to drive with conspicuous carelessness; the prospect of injury remains a powerful deterrent regardless of coverage. Moreover, the alternative to protection is not always prudence. Without insurance or emergency support, a single misfortune can ruin a family or a firm, producing harms that may dwarf the costs of the additional risk-taking.

For this reason, institutions rarely eliminate protection altogether. Instead, they design it to preserve some exposure to loss. Deductibles and co-payments ensure that the insured still bear part of any damage, and regulators may require rescued firms to replace their executives or accept strict conditions. The aim is not to abolish the safety net, but to ensure that those beneath it still have reason to watch their step.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what is the purpose of a deductible?
options: To keep the insured partly exposed to loss
To lower the price of an insurance policy
To reward drivers who have no accidents
To replace the executives of rescued firms
questions.why: Paragraph 4: deductibles ensure the insured still bear part of the damage.

questions.stem: In paragraph 1, what does diligent mean?
questions.why: A fully insured homeowner may be less careful about wiring and locks.

questions.stem: Which situation best illustrates moral hazard as the passage defines it?
options: A fully insured renter stops locking the door
A driver slows down after seeing an accident
A bank raises interest rates to slow its lending
A family saves money in case of a job loss
questions.why: Protection from loss leads to taking more risk.

questions.stem: Which sentence best summarizes the passage?
options: Protection can encourage risk, so it's designed to leave some cost.
Insurance should be abolished because it causes people to act carelessly.
Bank bailouts in 2008 were the main cause of the financial crisis.
Moral hazard is easy to measure, so economists agree on how to fix it.
questions.why: It defines the problem, notes its limits, and ends on how protection is designed.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention insured drivers in paragraph 3?
options: To show the effect can be weaker than theory says
To prove that insurance makes roads more dangerous
To explain how deductibles were first invented
To argue that drivers should not buy insurance
questions.why: Insured drivers don't drive conspicuously carelessly, so the effect is hard to see in practice.

passages.title: When the Number Becomes the Goal
paragraphs: In 1975, the British economist Charles Goodhart observed that any statistic the government relied on to manage the economy tended to lose its reliability once officials began targeting it. His insight, later condensed into the maxim "when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure," has since been applied far beyond economics, to schools, hospitals, and nearly every modern organization that runs on metrics.

The underlying mechanism is straightforward. A measure is useful because it correlates with something we genuinely care about but cannot observe directly. Test scores roughly track learning; the number of calls a support agent closes roughly tracks helpfulness. Once people are rewarded for the number itself, however, they discover ways to raise it that do not improve, and may even undermine, the underlying goal. Teachers drill students on the format of the exam rather than the subject, and support agents hurry callers off the phone in order to close more tickets.

A frequently repeated story, probably apocryphal, illustrates the point. A factory instructed to maximize the number of nails it produced made millions of tiny, useless ones; when the target was changed to total weight, it produced a few enormous nails instead. The tale endures because it exaggerates something real: those being measured usually understand the measurement better than those who designed it.

None of this implies that organizations should abandon measurement, which would leave them navigating blind. The more modest lesson is to treat any single number with suspicion, to track several indicators that are difficult to game simultaneously, and to keep looking directly at the work itself. A dashboard is a map of the territory, not the territory.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why is a measure useful in the first place?
options: It tracks something we can't see directly
It is simple for outsiders to understand
It can't be changed once it is recorded
It lets leaders reward their best workers
questions.why: Paragraph 2: a measure correlates with something we care about but can't observe directly.

questions.stem: In paragraph 3, what does apocryphal mean?
questions.why: The story is repeated often but probably didn't happen.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, which change would most likely make a support team's numbers harder to game?
options: Tracking both call counts and customer ratings
Raising the bonus for each ticket an agent closes
Measuring only the number of calls answered
Letting agents choose which calls to count
questions.why: Paragraph 4: track several indicators that are difficult to game at the same time.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the main idea?
options: Rewarding a number distorts it; use several and look at the work.
Organizations should stop using numbers to judge performance altogether.
Goodhart's law applies to economic statistics but rarely to schools.
Factories often cheat on targets, so their output can't be measured.
questions.why: It explains the distortion, then gives the modest lesson. It rejects abandoning measurement.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the story about the nail factory?
options: To exaggerate a real problem in a memorable way
To give historical proof that targets always fail
To show that factories are harder to measure
To criticize how Goodhart reached his conclusion
questions.why: "The tale endures because it exaggerates something real."
